content.topicNotes: Vertebrates Animals can be divided into vertebrates and invertebrates. Vertebrates have a backbone, and can be further divided into five classes. Mammals Mammals have mammary (milk) glands, sweat glands and give birth to live young. They also have four limbs and hair or fur. Humans, dolphins and bears are mammals. Birds Birds have feathers, two wings and two legs (which have scales). They lay hard-shelled eggs on land and they have lightweight bones. Penguins, sparrows and eagles are birds. Reptiles Reptiles lay waterproof eggs on land and, excluding snakes, have four limbs. They have dry, scaly skin. Crocodiles, turtles and chameleons are reptiles. Amphibians Amphibians lay eggs covered in jelly, in water. They have moist scale-less skin, often have webbed feet, and perform gas exchange through their lungs and skin. Newts and frogs are amphibians. Fish Fish have scales, fins and a lateral line (a line that runs down the middle of their bodies). They have gills for gas exchange in water. Sharks, salmon and clownfish are all fish. Vertebrates Vertebrates can be classified into five classes: Mammals Reptiles Birds Amphibians Fish
content.description: Biology: Cambridge International GCSE Core > Characteristics of Living Organisms > Features of Organisms

content.topicNotes: Vitamins and Minerals A ‘balanced diet’ is one where all the nutritional requirements of the body are met, and includes the following vitamins and minerals: Vitamin C Vitamin C is important for making collagen (an important protein in blood vessels and skin). Vitamin C prevents scurvy. Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits (e.g. lemons and oranges) as well as some other fruits like strawberries. Vitamin D Vitamin D is needed for absorbing calcium and phosphorous, which is important for keeping bones healthy. Vitamin D prevents rickets. Vitamin D is found in oily fish, egg yolks and shiitake mushrooms. Iron Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen around the body in red blood cells. Iron is found in red meats, liver and nuts. Calcium Calcium is important for growing bones and teeth. Calcium is found in dairy (e.g. milk) and green vegetables (e.g. broccoli).
content.description: Biology: Cambridge International GCSE Core > Human Nutrition > Diet

content.topicNotes: Non-Biodegradable Plastics Non-biodegradable plastics can last unchanged for many hundreds of years, polluting aquatic (water) and terrestrial (land) systems. Ingestion of solid plastics Animals that ingest (eat) plastics may perforate (make holes in) their digestive systems and/or block their respiratory systems, leading to death. Leaching of toxic substanes Toxic substances can leach out (drain away from soil) and directly poison living organisms.

content.topicNotes: Water Water is a very important solvent (things can be dissolved in it) in living organisms. This means substances can be transported in it, and chemical reactions can take place in it. The chemical symbol for water is H2O; it is made of the elements hydrogen and oxygen. Transport Blood is made mainly of water, with many substances (such as soluble food particles) dissolved in it and transported around the body. Waste products such as excess salt are dissolved in urine (which is mainly water), and passed out of the body. Reactions Most human digestive enzymes (proteins that break down large food particles) only work when dissolved in water. Water Water is vital for processes in living organisms. Water is the universal solvent for living organisms, and therefore necessary for life. It is important for transporting dissolved substances. It is the solvent for many chemical reactions in organisms.
content.description: Biology: Cambridge International GCSE Core > Movement Into & Out of Cells > Osmosis

content.topicNotes: Water Pathway Water moves into the plant in the roots, then moves up through the plant: Root hair cell First, water osmoses into root hair cells. These are specialised cells on roots that have projections, creating a large surface area for osmosis. Root cortex cells Water then moves into the root cortex cells. Xylem vessels Xylem vessels collect water from the root cortex and transport it up the plant's stem. Mesophyll cells When it reaches a leaf, water osmoses out of the xylem into the leaf's mesophyll cells. Investigating the pathway By putting a wilting celery stalk in water that contains a stain such as blue food dye, it is possible to watch the blue water travelling up the celery stem and to the leaves.
content.description: Biology: Cambridge International GCSE Core > Transport in Plants > Water Uptake

content.topicNotes: White Bloods Cells White blood cells defend against infections. There are two types of white blood cells; phagocytes and lymphocytes. Have a nucleus Unlike red blood cells, white blood cells have a nucleus. Can change shape White blood cells can change shape. This allows them to squeeze through the walls of blood vessels into body tissues.
content.description: Biology: Cambridge International GCSE Core > Transport in Animals > Blood

content.topicNotes: Xylem Cell The xylem is specialised to transport water up the stem of a plant and into the leaves. Open ended cells Xylem vessels are made up of a series of connected dead xylem cells. The end walls of the dead cells are broken to allow water to move through. Lignin Lignin (a substance) strengthens the cell walls of xylem cells.
